characters: Ashitey: a caring ten-year-old Ghanaian boy with short neat hair, wearing a light-blue polo shirt at home and a yellow-and-brown Primary 4 uniform at school.
Quaicoe: his three-year-old cousin, a small Ghanaian toddler in a soft green cotton t-shirt.
Quaicoe’s mother: a gentle Ghanaian aunt in a warm terracotta-and-gold patterned wrap skirt and top.
The clinic nurse: a kind Ghanaian community health nurse with neat braided hair, wearing a clean teal scrub uniform.

narrationPlan.voice: A caring boy’s voice for Ashitey; a calm, reassuring woman’s voice for the clinic nurse
narrationPlan.pace: Calm and caring, never frightening (about 100 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

culturalNotes: Follows the NaCCA Basic 4 Science standard on the causes, symptoms, and prevention of measles (B4.5.2.1.1) and Ghana Health Service Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) guidance (measles-rubella vaccination recorded in the Child Health Record booklet).
Reassures learners without fear or stigma: measles is caused by an airborne virus, requires prompt clinic care rather than unverified home remedies, and is preventable through routine vaccination.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Confirm symptoms (fever, cough, runny nose, red watery eyes, rash spreading from the face downward) and prevention guidance against Ghana Health Service / EPI materials.
Check that the tone remains calm, non-stigmatising, and supportive.

teacherGuide.overview: Through a caring family story, learners discover that measles is caused by an airborne virus, learn its early signs, and understand how clinic care, temporary isolation while contagious, and routine measles vaccination protect communities. Based on NaCCA Basic 4 Science.
learningGoals: State that measles is caused by a virus spread through coughs and sneezes.
Identify four key signs of measles (fever, cough/runny nose, red watery eyes, and rash).
Explain how vaccination, prompt clinic visits, and respiratory hygiene prevent measles.

subjectLinks.subject: Science (NaCCA B4.5.2.1.1)
subjectLinks.link: Causes, symptoms, and prevention of measles

beforeReading: Ask: why do babies and young children visit child-welfare clinics (“weighing”) even when they look healthy?
whileReading: Pause on page 3 to reinforce how respiratory droplets travel and why blame has no place in illness.
afterReading: Draw a three-branch visual map showing Measles: Cause, Signs, and Prevention.
Invite the school SHEP coordinator or a community health nurse to speak with the class.
discussion: Why should a child with measles rest at home away from school until the nurse says they have recovered?
How does vaccination protect younger babies in the neighbourhood too?
reflection: What should you do right away if a younger sibling or friend develops a high fever and a rash?

support: Match simple icon cards into two groups: “Signs of Measles” and “Ways to Prevent Measles”.
stretch: Learn how Ghana’s Child Health Record booklet tracks two doses of the measles-rubella vaccine in early childhood.

culturalNotes: Follows the NaCCA Basic 4 Science standard on the causes, symptoms, and prevention of measles (B4.5.2.1.1) and Ghana Health Service Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) guidance (measles-rubella vaccination recorded in the Child Health Record booklet).
Reassures learners without fear or stigma: measles is caused by an airborne virus, requires prompt clinic care rather than unverified home remedies, and is preventable through routine vaccination.
localiseThis: Refer to your local CHPS compound, health centre, or polyclinic.
Handle illness discussions sensitively, never singling out any learner’s personal medical history.

factCheck.claim: Measles is a highly contagious airborne viral disease characterised by high fever, cough, coryza (runny nose), conjunctivitis (red watery eyes), and a maculopapular rash starting on the face, and is effectively prevented by routine measles vaccination.
factCheck.explanation: Matches WHO and Ghana Health Service clinical case definitions and Expanded Programme on Immunisation (EPI) schedules.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA Science Curriculum for Basic 4 (B4.5.2.1.1), Ghana Health Service EPI, & WHO Measles Fact Sheet.
